title: Maximum Degree-Based Quasi-Clique Search via an Iterative Framework

problem.claim: The paper addresses maximum γ-quasi-clique search, where each vertex must connect to at least a γ proportion of the other vertices in the subgraph.

gap.claim: The problem is NP-hard, lacks the hereditary property needed for effective pruning, and existing algorithms have scalability or low-γ performance limitations.

contributions.claim: IterQC reformulates maximum γ-quasi-clique search as a series of k-plex problems with the hereditary property.
IterQC uses an iterative framework with pseudo lower bounds that transfer information across iterations to improve branch-and-bound efficiency.
IterQC applies preprocessing to reduce problem size and unnecessary iterations.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe IterQC as a novel algorithm and its iterative framework as non-trivial.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that IterQC achieves up to four orders of magnitude speedup over DDA and FastQC.
The authors report that IterQC solves significantly more graph instances than DDA and FastQC.
The authors describe the evaluation as extensive experiments.

narrative_sequence.summary: Cohesive subgraph mining is presented as a fundamental graph-theory problem with applications including social networks and protein interactions.
The γ-quasi-clique is introduced as a flexible cohesive subgraph defined by a minimum connection proportion.
Maximum γ-quasi-clique search is difficult because it is NP-hard and lacks the hereditary property needed for efficient pruning.
DDA and FastQC are described as having scalability problems or declining performance at small γ values.
IterQC reformulates the problem through k-plexes, adds iterative optimizations, and is reported to outperform the comparison algorithms in experiments.

source_observation.claim: The proposed method converts the target problem into a sequence of related problems with a hereditary property and transfers information between iterations.

interpretation.claim: When direct pruning is difficult, reformulation plus cross-iteration information may create exploitable structure.

application.claim: This pattern may apply to iterative exact-search systems whose successive subproblems can share bounds or other state.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the approach generalizes beyond maximum γ-quasi-clique search or which graph families benefit most.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, graph sizes, parameter ranges, hardware, or experimental protocol.
The abstract does not quantify baseline runtimes, solved-instance counts, or the conditions producing the reported speedup.
The abstract does not provide correctness proofs or detailed complexity analysis.
